title: Particles: where sugar goes when it dissolves

summary.text: Stir a spoon of sugar into water, and the grains vanish. Yet the water tastes sweet, and it weighs just as much as the water and sugar did before. The sugar has broken into particles far too small to see, and they have spread all through the water. Everything around us is made of particles like these: sugar, water, air, a steel tumbler and you. In this unit your child weighs dissolved sugar on a home-made balance, races a kalkandu lump against powdered sugar, and asks ants to find sugar that nobody can see.
summary.art: A clear steel-rimmed glass of water with a spoon of sugar pouring in, and beside it a zoomed-in circle showing tiny round water particles with a few sugar particles spread among them.

intro.hook: Drop a spoon of sugar into a clear glass of water and stir. In a minute the grains are gone, and the water looks just like plain water. Is the sugar still in there? If it is, where is it?
intro.text: Most people say the sugar has 'melted' or 'gone'. Neither is right. In this unit you find out what really happens. You test it three ways: by tasting, by weighing, and by asking ants. You also find out that sugar, water and everything else are made of tiny pieces called particles, and why some sugar dissolves faster than other sugar.
intro.art: A child's face close to a clear glass of water, looking hard for the sugar that just disappeared, with a spoon still in the glass.

outcomes: I can say that everything around me, solid, liquid or gas, is made of particles far too small to see.
I can explain what happens when sugar dissolves: water particles pull sugar particles off the grain, one by one, and they spread through the water.
I can show with a balance and by tasting that dissolved sugar is still there, and still weighs the same.
I can run a fair test to find whether a lump, grains or powder of sugar dissolves fastest, and explain why.
I can tell dissolving from melting, and give an example of each.
I can tell how people found out that a dissolved thing is still there, and what the old idea was: that it stops existing.

terms.meaning: A very tiny piece that a material is made of. Particles are far too small to see, even with a magnifying glass.
terms.example: A single grain of sugar is made of a huge number of sugar particles, packed together.
terms.art: A sugar grain drawn big, with a zoomed-in corner showing neat rows of tiny round particles.

terms.meaning: When a solid breaks up into its particles in a liquid and spreads through it, we say the solid dissolves. You can no longer see it, but it is still there.
terms.example: Sugar dissolves in tea. Salt dissolves in rasam.
terms.art: A spoon of sugar in a glass of water, shown in three pictures: grains at the bottom, fewer grains, then clear water.

terms.meaning: The clear mixture you get when something dissolves in a liquid.
terms.example: Sugar water is a solution. So is salty water.
terms.art: Two clear glasses that look the same, labelled plain water and sugar solution.

terms.meaning: A solid whose particles are stacked in a neat, repeating pattern. Crystals often have flat sides and sharp corners.
terms.example: Each grain of sugar is a small crystal. Kalkandu, or rock sugar, is made of big sugar crystals.
terms.art: A clear kalkandu crystal with flat shining faces, next to a few grains of sugar seen through a magnifying glass.

terms.meaning: When a solid gets hot enough to turn into a liquid on its own. Melting needs heat, not water.
terms.example: Ghee melts in a warm pan. Ice melts on a hot day.
terms.art: A spoon of solid ghee turning to golden liquid in a warm pan.

terms.meaning: The scientists' name for the smallest particle of a substance like sugar or water. A molecule is made of even smaller atoms joined together.
terms.example: One sugar molecule is the smallest piece of sugar there can be.
terms.art: A drawing of one sugar molecule as a small cluster of joined balls, with a label 'one sugar particle'.

terms.meaning: A tool that compares how heavy two things are. The heavier side goes down.
terms.example: A shopkeeper's pan balance weighs vegetables against iron weights.
terms.art: A coat hanger hanging from a door handle with a bag on each end, one side lower.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: To see which sugar dissolves fastest, use the same water, the same glasses and the same stirring for each.
terms.art: Three identical glasses in a row, each with a different kind of sugar on a spoon above it.

terms.meaning: Something we make or draw to help us think about a thing we cannot see or hold.
terms.example: Beans on a plate can be a model of the particles in a sugar grain.
terms.art: A plate with a square of rajma beans surrounded by rice grains.

explanations.context: This card says what everything is made of.
explanations.definition: Every material, solid, liquid or gas, is made of particles that are far too small to see. Different materials are made of different particles.
explanations.description: A sugar particle is about a millionth of a millimetre across. Even the best ordinary microscope cannot show one. In a solid, the particles are packed close and hold their places, so a solid keeps its shape. In a liquid, they are close but slide past each other, so a liquid flows. In a gas, like air, they are far apart and fly about. Particles never stop moving, even in a stone.
examples: A grain of sugar holds roughly a million million million sugar particles. That is a 1 with 18 zeros.
Air is made of particles too. You feel them push when the wind blows.
Your body is made of particles: water, sugars, fats and many more.
explanations.art: Three boxes side by side: particles packed in neat rows for a solid, particles close but jumbled for a liquid, and a few particles far apart for a gas.

explanations.context: This card explains what happens to sugar in water.
explanations.definition: When sugar dissolves, water particles attract the sugar particles on the outside of a grain and pull them away, one by one. The sugar particles then spread out among the water particles.
explanations.description: Water particles bump and tug at a sugar grain from every side. They can only reach the particles on its outside. As the outside particles leave, the next ones are uncovered, so the grain gets smaller and smaller until it is gone. Each sugar particle is now surrounded by water particles. It is far too small to see, but it is still sugar. That is why the water tastes sweet.
examples: Sugar in a glass of lemon juice dissolves in about a minute if you stir it.
Salt dissolves in sambar, so you taste it everywhere but cannot see it.
explanations.art: A sugar grain drawn as a block of tiny particles, with water particles pulling particles off its corners and edges and carrying them away.

explanations.context: This card is about the balance test, where you weighed sugar before and after it dissolved.
explanations.concept: Dissolved sugar still weighs the same
explanations.definition: When something dissolves, nothing is lost. The solution weighs exactly as much as the liquid and the solid did before.
explanations.description: Every sugar particle that left the grain is still in the bottle. So the weight cannot change. This is true for every kind of change in a closed bottle, even melting and burning: the total weight stays the same. Scientists call this the conservation of mass. Mass means how much stuff there is.
examples: 100 grams of water and 16 grams of sugar make 116 grams of sugar water.
An ice cube in a closed box weighs the same after it melts.
explanations.art: A bottle of water and a paper packet of sugar on one pan of a balance, and the same bottle of clear sugar water with the empty paper on the same pan, both balanced level.

explanations.context: This card sorts out two words people often mix up.
explanations.definition: Melting is a solid turning into a liquid because it is heated. Dissolving is a solid breaking up into its particles inside a liquid.
explanations.description: People often say sugar 'melts' in tea. It does not. Sugar dissolves even in cold water, with no heat at all. To melt sugar, you have to heat it in a dry pan to about 186 degrees Celsius, much hotter than boiling water. Then it turns into a thick liquid that becomes caramel. Melting needs only one substance. Dissolving always needs two: one that dissolves and one that it dissolves in.
examples: Ice melts into water on a hot day. Nothing else is needed.
Sugar dissolves in cold water from the fridge. No heat is needed.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: sugar grains in a dry pan on a flame turning brown and runny, and sugar in a glass of cold water disappearing.

explanations.context: This card is about the race between a kalkandu lump, sugar grains and powdered sugar.
explanations.definition: Sugar dissolves faster when it is crushed small, when it is stirred, and when the water is warm.
explanations.description: Water can only pull particles off the outside of a piece. Crush a lump into powder, and the same sugar has far more outside, so many more particles leave at once. Stirring helps because the sweet water next to the sugar is carried away, and fresh water takes its place. Warm water helps because its particles move faster and tug harder.
examples: Powdered sugar vanishes in seconds. A lump of kalkandu can take many minutes.
Jaggery is grated or crushed before it goes into panakam, the South Indian jaggery drink.
explanations.art: One big sugar cube beside the same cube crushed into many small pieces, with arrows showing water reaching every small piece from all sides.

explanations.context: This card is about the tall glass test, where sugar lay at the bottom without stirring.
explanations.concept: Particles move, but spread slowly on their own
explanations.definition: Particles in a liquid are always moving and bumping. This slowly spreads dissolved particles out, even with no stirring. Scientists call this spreading diffusion.
explanations.description: Diffusion through water is very slow. Sugar left unstirred at the bottom of a tall glass can take many days to spread to the top on its own. So the top stays plain while the bottom is very sweet. Stirring spreads it in seconds. In air, smells spread faster, because air moves about and its particles have more space.
examples: Unstirred sugar in tea makes the last sip the sweetest.
The smell of jasmine flowers spreads across a room in a few minutes, carried by moving air.
explanations.art: A tall glass of water with a thick, clear, shimmering layer at the bottom, and a straw dipping into it.

explanations.context: This card asks what particles are made of, which goes beyond this unit.
explanations.description: A sugar particle is made of 45 atoms joined together: 12 of carbon, 22 of hydrogen and 11 of oxygen. Atoms are made of even smaller particles. Physicists now describe those smallest particles as ripples in fields that fill all of space. Nobody knows yet whether there is anything deeper still. That is why this card says 'idea'.
examples: A water particle is made of 3 atoms: 2 of hydrogen and 1 of oxygen.
Sugar and the paper in a book are made of the same three kinds of atom, joined in different ways.
explanations.art: A zoom in four circles: a sugar grain, a sugar particle as a cluster of 45 balls, one atom, and a faint shimmering field.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree that everything is made of particles.
agreed.text: Everything is made of particles far too small to see.
agreed.evidence: Scientists first worked it out from how gases and dissolved things behave. Since the 1980s, special microscopes have made pictures of single atoms.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree that dissolved sugar is still there.
agreed.text: A dissolved substance is still there, as particles spread through the liquid.
agreed.evidence: The solution tastes of the dissolved substance. It weighs more than the liquid alone by exactly the weight of that substance. When the liquid dries up, the substance is left behind.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree that the total weight stays the same in a closed container.
agreed.text: In a closed container, the total weight stays the same through dissolving, melting and chemical changes.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have weighed this carefully since the 1700s, and it has always held.

agreed.context: This card says scientists agree on what makes sugar dissolve faster.
agreed.text: Crushing, stirring and warming make a solid dissolve faster.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it at home with sugar or salt.

challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake.
challenging.claim: When sugar dissolves, it is gone.
challenging.who: A very common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: You cannot see the sugar any more, and the water looks plain.
challenging.against: The water tastes sweet, weighs more by exactly the weight of the sugar, and ants come to it. The sugar is still there, as particles too small to see.

challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake.
challenging.who: A very common way of speaking
challenging.for: The grains seem to turn into liquid and run away, a bit like ice melting.
challenging.against: Sugar dissolves even in ice-cold water. Melting sugar needs a dry pan at about 186 degrees Celsius. Dissolving needs water. Melting needs heat.

challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that lasted a long time.
challenging.claim: When two things truly mix, each stops being itself, and a new thing takes the place of both.
challenging.who: Followers of the Greek thinker Aristotle, for about 2,000 years
challenging.for: A solution looks like one new, even liquid. You cannot see two things in it.
challenging.against: In the early 1600s, Daniel Sennert dissolved silver in a strong acid and got the same silver back. The silver had been there all along, as tiny particles.

challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that lasted until about 1910.
challenging.claim: Particles are not real. They are only a handy way of thinking.
challenging.who: Some famous scientists around 1900, such as Wilhelm Ostwald and Ernst Mach
challenging.for: Nobody had ever seen a particle, and some said science should talk only about what can be measured.
challenging.against: Experiments around 1908 measured how particles bump into specks in water, and worked out their size. Ostwald changed his mind. Today, microscopes can make pictures of single atoms.

challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make in the hanger balance test.
challenging.claim: Dissolved sugar weighs less, because it has become thin and spread out.
challenging.who: A common guess before the hanger balance test
challenging.for: Spread out, the sugar seems lighter, like a cloud compared with a stone.
challenging.against: Every particle is still in the bottle, and each one weighs just what it did. The balance stays level.

big_questions.q: If you keep crushing sugar into smaller and smaller pieces, is there a smallest piece that is still sugar?
big_questions.hint: Scientists say yes: one sugar particle, a molecule. Break that, and you have atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which are not sweet.

big_questions.q: When the sugar spread through the water, was it one thing or many things?
big_questions.hint: Think about the heap on the spoon, and then the same sugar spread out in every sip.

big_questions.q: If something is too small for anyone to see, how can we be sure it is there?
big_questions.hint: In this unit you used your tongue, a balance and some ants. What other ways can you think of?

big_questions.q: Ants found the sugar water and left the plain water alone. What else might be around us that other living beings notice and we do not?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dog's nose, a bee's eyes, or a snake that senses warmth.

big_questions.q: The particles in a stone floor never stop moving. So is anything really still?
big_questions.hint: The floor looks still because its particles jiggle in place and do not go anywhere.

big_questions.q: The sugar particles in your tea came from a sugarcane field, and before that from air, water and sunlight. Where were the particles in your body before they were you?
big_questions.hint: Think about the food you ate this week, and where that food came from.

story.title: The Sour Glass at Chithi's Stall
story.note: Kavya, her aunt Meenakshi, the stall and the customer are made up. Juice stalls in India often keep a bottle of sugar syrup, and unstirred syrup really does stay at the bottom of a glass.
text: Every summer holiday, Kavya helped at her Chithi's juice stall near the bus stand in Madurai. Chithi means aunt, and Kavya's Chithi was called Meenakshi. Her stall sold lemon juice, sugarcane juice and sweet lime juice. It had a steel counter, a big glass jar of lemons, and a tall bottle of thick, clear sugar syrup.

Kavya was nine. Her job was to squeeze the lemons, pour in the syrup, fill the glass with cold water and hand it over. It was May, and the queue never ended. There were bus drivers, students, and a grandmother with a basket of jasmine flowers. Everyone was hot and thirsty.

That afternoon a bus conductor came to the counter. He wore a khaki uniform and a leather bag across his chest, and he looked tired. 'One lemon juice, please,' he said, 'and hurry, my bus leaves in five minutes.'

Kavya squeezed half a lemon into a glass. She poured in a long stream of syrup. She filled the glass slowly with water from the cold steel can and handed it over with a straw. Then she turned to the next customer.
'Hey!' The conductor held up his glass. 'You forgot the sugar. This is sour as anything.'
'I put it in,' said Kavya. 'I poured the syrup myself.'
The conductor held the glass up to the light. 'Where? I see only water and lemon pips. There is no sugar in here.'
Kavya looked at the glass too. He was right that she could not see any sugar. The water was clear all the way down. But she had poured the syrup. She was sure of it. So where had it gone?

Then she noticed something. Near the bottom of the glass, the water looked a little different. It shimmered, the way air shimmers above a hot road. It was like a clear, wobbly layer, sitting under the rest.

Kavya also noticed the ants. A line of small black ants was marching along the counter to a sticky ring where an earlier glass had stood. They were not going to the wet ring of the water can. They were going only to the ring where syrup had dripped. They could find the sugar even in a ring she could hardly see.
'Wait,' said Kavya. 'Please don't drink from the top. Give me one second.'

She took a clean straw. She put her finger tight over its top end and pushed it straight down to the very bottom of his glass. Then she lifted her finger. A little water rushed up into the straw. She pressed her finger down again, lifted the straw out, and let the drops fall onto a clean steel spoon.
'Taste this,' she said. 'This is from the bottom.'
The conductor tasted it. His eyebrows went up. 'That is sweet. Very sweet.'

'The sugar is all at the bottom,' said Kavya. 'The syrup is heavy, so it sank, and I forgot to stir. The top is just lemon and water.' She took a long spoon and stirred the glass round and round, ten times. 'Now try it.'
He sipped. He smiled for the first time. 'Now that is lemon juice.' Then he frowned. 'But I still can't see any sugar. Did you add more while I wasn't looking?'
'No,' said Kavya. 'It was in there all the time. You just can't see it.'
He laughed, paid, and ran for his bus, still drinking.
That night, Chithi and Kavya washed the glasses together. Kavya told her what had happened. 'Chithi, how can sugar be in the water if you can't see it? Where does it hide?'

Chithi dried her hands. 'It doesn't hide. It breaks up. A grain of sugar is made of tiny pieces called particles, far too small to see. The water pulls those particles apart and they spread out among the water's own particles. Each one is too small to see, but each one is still sugar.'
'So the syrup was sugar particles too?' said Kavya.

'Yes. Lots of them, packed into a little water. That makes syrup heavy, so it sinks if you don't stir. The particles do move about on their own, but very, very slowly. Left alone, they would take days to spread to the top.'
Kavya thought about the ants on the counter. 'The ants knew the sugar was there. They didn't need to see it.'
'Ants sense the world with their antennae,' said Chithi. 'They smell and taste with them. They found the particles that you couldn't see.'
The next morning, Kavya wrote a sign in big letters and stuck it on the syrup bottle: STIR TEN TIMES. Under it, smaller, she wrote: The sugar is always there. You just can't see it.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the conductor tasted the top of an unstirred glass. The sugar had already dissolved in the syrup, so it was invisible, but the syrup is denser than water and sank to the bottom. Sugar particles do spread on their own by diffusion, but through water this takes days, so the top stayed sour. The shimmering layer was the syrup bending light differently from the water above it. Kavya's straw trick took a sample from the bottom. Stirring spread the particles through the whole glass in seconds. The ants found a sugar ring that was almost invisible, because they sense sugar with their antennae.
ask: Why did the top of the conductor's glass taste sour, even though Kavya had poured in the syrup?
How did Kavya take water from only the bottom of the glass?
The conductor still could not see the sugar after stirring. How do you know it was there?
The ants went to the syrup ring but not the water ring. What does that tell you about the ants?
The conductor said there was no sugar because he could not see any. Is seeing a good way to decide if something is there?

printables.title: 4 'Where it went' cards to cut out
items: Into water, a drink or food

rules: Lay the 4 'Where it went' cards face up in a row.
Take out the camphor card for the practice round. Shuffle the other 15 'It disappeared' cards and make a pile with the story side up.
On your turn, take the top card and read it aloud.
Put it on the 'Where it went' card that fits. Then say what the thing broke into: grains, crumbs or particles.
Turn the card over to check. If you put it in the right place, keep the card and score 1 point. If you also said the word 'particles' in your reason, score 1 more point.
If you put it in the wrong place, the card is out of the game and nobody keeps it.
Some cards can fit two places. If you can explain your choice, it counts as right.
When all 15 cards are used, count your points. The most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
If you play alone, try to keep all 15 cards and give a 'particles' reason for each one. That makes 30 points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay the 4 'Where it went' cards face up. 3. Take out the camphor card. Shuffle the other 15 cards and put them in a pile, story side up.
flow.say: Every card is about something that seems to vanish. Nothing really vanishes. Your job is to say where it went.
flow.kid: Lay the 'Where it went' cards face up. Shuffle the other cards in a pile. Every card is something that seems to vanish. Where did it really go?
flow.context: This is the start of Where Did It Go?, a card game about things that seem to disappear.

flow.do: Play the camphor card together as a practice round. Nobody keeps it.
flow.say: Practice card. A camphor tablet left on a plate gets smaller every day. Where did the camphor go?
flow.kid: Practice card. A camphor tablet gets smaller every day. Where did it go?

check.q: A camphor tablet left on a plate gets smaller every day. Where did the camphor go?
options: Into the air, as camphor particles
check.why: Camphor particles leave the tablet and go into the air. That is why a room with camphor smells of it: the particles reach your nose. Picking 'destroyed' is the usual first guess, because we can't see where it went. Picking 'into the plate' is a good thought, but the plate stays dry and does not smell.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Read a card, place it, and give a reason. 3. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Read your card. Where did it go? Tell us what it broke into.
flow.kid: Read your card. Put it where it went. Say why. Turn the card over to check.
flow.parent: Help your child use the word 'particles' in their reasons, for example 'the sugar broke into particles that spread through the tea'. The chappal and eraser cards are about tiny crumbs, not single particles. That is fine. Crumbs are made of particles too.

flow.do: Count the cards and points. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Was there any card where the thing was really gone, with nothing left anywhere?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Was anything really gone, with nothing left anywhere?
flow.think: Can you think of anything that disappears and is truly gone?
flow.parent: A good answer is no. In every case, the stuff went somewhere, as crumbs or particles. Scientists have weighed things before and after such changes for over 200 years, and nothing is lost.

games.title: Dissolve Race: a bean board game
games.context: This is a board game with beans. A square of beans is a model of a sugar grain, and you play the water. Water can only pull off the beans it touches, so the game shows why crushed sugar dissolves faster.

printables.title: A mat with a 5 by 5 square of 25 circles: the sugar grain (print one for each player)
4 dice key cards to stick on the table
items: 1 or 2: Still water. Take 1 bean for every 4 beans that touch the water.
3 or 4: Stir! Take 1 bean for every 2 beans that touch the water.
5: Warm water! Take 3 beans for every 4 beans that touch the water.
6: Crush! Take no beans. Pull your grain apart into small pieces with gaps, so that empty space is beside every bean.

printables.title: Beans and a dice
items: Use 25 rajma or chana beans for each player, or cut 25 small paper circles. You also need one dice and a small bowl for each player.

rules: Two players, or two teams if more play. Each side has a mat, 25 beans and a bowl. Put a bean on every circle: this is your sugar grain. The empty paper around the mat is the water.
A bean touches the water when there is empty space on at least one of its sides: up, down, left or right.
On your turn, count the beans that touch the water. Roll the dice and read the dice key.
Take the number of beans the key says, only from the beans that touch the water, and put them in your bowl. They have dissolved. Round down, but always take at least 1.
On a 6, take no beans. Pull your grain apart into small pieces with gaps, until empty space is beside every bean. Now many more beans touch the water.
The first side to dissolve all of its beans wins. If the other side finishes in the same round, it is a tie.

flow.do: 1. Give each side a mat, 25 beans and a bowl. 2. Put a bean on every circle. 3. Point to the beans on the edge, and then to the 9 in the middle.
flow.say: This square of beans is a sugar grain, and each bean is a sugar particle. You are the water. Water can only reach the beans on the outside.
flow.kid: Put a bean on every circle. This is a sugar grain. You are the water. Can you reach the beans in the middle?
flow.context: This is the start of Dissolve Race, a bean game. The square of beans is a model of a sugar grain.

flow.do: Ask how many beans touch the water now.
flow.say: How many beans are on the outside, touching the water? Count them.
flow.kid: Count the beans on the outside. How many touch the water?

check.q: A 5 by 5 square has 25 beans. How many touch the water at the start?
check.why: The outside ring has 16 beans. The 9 in the middle are covered on every side. Picking 'all 25' means forgetting that water can only reach the outside. Picking 9 counts the middle instead of the edge.

flow.do: 1. Take turns counting, rolling and taking beans. 2. On a 6, pull the grain apart into pieces.
flow.say: Count the beans that touch the water. Roll the dice. Take only beans that touch the water.
flow.kid: Count the beans touching the water. Roll the dice. Take beans from the outside only. On a 6, pull your grain apart!
flow.parent: Watch for the first 6. After the grain is pulled apart, every bean touches the water, so the next rolls take many more beans. That is what crushing does to real sugar.

flow.do: Talk about the game.
flow.say: When did the beans go fastest? Why does crushing sugar make it dissolve faster?
flow.kid: When did your beans go fastest? Why?

ask.q: Why does crushing sugar make it dissolve faster?
good: More of it is on the outside.
The water can reach more particles at once.

experiments.title: The Hanger Balance: does vanished sugar still weigh anything?
experiments.question: When sugar dissolves and we can't see it any more, is it still there? Does it still weigh anything?
experiments.predict: Guess first. We will weigh a bottle of water with some sugar beside it. Then we will dissolve the sugar and weigh it again. Will it be lighter, the same, or heavier? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everything that was on side A before stays on side A: the bottle, its cap, the water, the sugar and its paper. Nothing is added and nothing is taken away. The only change is that the sugar is dissolved instead of in grains. The bottle stays closed, so nothing can escape.

materials.item: 2 identical small plastic bottles with caps, such as two empty 200 or 500 millilitre water bottles
a plastic coat hanger with a hook, and a door handle, or a broom handle laid across the backs of two chairs, to hang it from
2 small polythene bags or cloth bags with handles, the same kind
a drinking straw, some sticky tape, and a sheet of paper
sugar: 4 level teaspoons
a small cup to measure water, and a teaspoon
a clean steel spoon for tasting
optional: a digital kitchen scale

schedule.what: Make a hanger balance. Balance a bottle of water and a packet of sugar against another bottle. Dissolve the sugar in the closed bottle and weigh again. Taste it.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the hanger before and after the sugar dissolved, with the pointer.

flow.do: 1. Hang the coat hanger from a door handle, or from a broom handle across two chairs. 2. Tape the straw to the middle of the hanger so it points straight down. 3. Tape the paper on the door or a chair behind the straw tip. 4. Hang one bag from each end of the hanger.
flow.say: We are making a balance. If one side gets heavier, it goes down, and the straw swings the other way.
flow.kid: Hang the hanger up. Tape the straw so it points down. Hang a bag on each end. The straw is your pointer.
flow.parent: A plastic hanger with notches at each end works best, because the bags cannot slide. If you only have a wire hanger, tape the bag handles in place at the two ends. Keep the bags clear of the door so they swing freely.
flow.context: This is the first step of the hanger balance experiment. Here you make a balance from a coat hanger, to weigh sugar before and after it dissolves.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 small cup of water into each bottle and close the caps. Call them A and B. 2. Put 4 level teaspoons of sugar on a square of paper, and fold it into a packet. 3. Put bottle A and the sugar packet in the left bag. Put bottle B in the right bag.
flow.say: Bottle A has the sugar with it. So which side do you think goes down?
flow.kid: Fill both bottles with one cup of water. Close them. Fold the sugar into a paper packet. Put bottle A and the sugar on the left. Put bottle B on the right.
flow.parent: Side A should go down, because it has the sugar too. 4 teaspoons of sugar weigh about 16 grams.

flow.do: 1. Open bottle B and add water a teaspoon at a time. 2. After each spoon, close it and hang it back. 3. Stop when the straw points straight down again. 4. Draw a line on the paper where the straw tip is.
flow.say: Now we add water to bottle B until both sides weigh the same. When the straw points straight down, they balance.
flow.kid: Add water to bottle B, one spoon at a time. Stop when the straw points straight down. Draw a line at the straw's tip.
flow.parent: It may take 3 or 4 teaspoons. Now try this: lift the sugar packet out of bag A. Side A goes up, and the straw swings. Put it back. This shows your balance can feel 4 teaspoons of sugar.

flow.do: Ask your child to predict before anything changes.
flow.say: Now we will pour the sugar into bottle A and shake it until it disappears. Then everything goes back in bag A. Will side A go up, stay level, or go down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will dissolve the sugar in bottle A. Then it goes back in the bag. Will side A go up, stay level or go down? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen, and why?
good: It will go up, because the sugar disappears.
It will stay level, because the sugar is still inside.
It will go down, because sugar water is heavier.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children, and many grown-ups, guess that side A will go up. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Take bottle A and the packet out. 2. Roll the packet's paper into a funnel and pour every grain into the bottle. Tap the paper. 3. Close the cap tight and shake for about 2 minutes, until no grains are left. 4. Put the bottle and the empty paper back in bag A.
flow.say: Pour in every grain, and keep the paper. Now shake until you can't see any sugar at all.
flow.kid: Pour all the sugar into bottle A. Keep the paper. Close the cap. Shake until the sugar is gone. Put it all back in the bag.
flow.parent: If a few grains spill, put them back into the bag too, so nothing is lost. 4 teaspoons dissolve in a cup of water in 1 or 2 minutes of shaking.

flow.do: 1. Let the hanger stop swinging. 2. Look at where the straw points.
flow.say: Look at the straw. Where does it point now?
flow.kid: Wait for the hanger to stop. Where does the straw point now?

check.q: The sugar vanished, but the straw still pointed at the line. What does this show?
options: The sugar is still in the bottle, and weighs just as much as before
check.why: Your balance could feel the sugar, because side A went up when you lifted the packet out. After dissolving, the sides still balanced. So all the sugar was still in the bottle, as particles too small to see. Picking 'gone' is the guess most people make, because we trust our eyes. Picking 'broken' is a good thought, but you tested the balance with the packet first.

flow.parent: With a kitchen scale, you can do the same thing in numbers: weigh bottle A with the packet beside it, then again after dissolving. The reading should not change.

flow.do: Pour a few drops from each bottle onto a clean steel spoon, and taste them.
flow.say: We can't see the sugar. But can we taste it?
flow.kid: Taste a drop from bottle A. Then one from bottle B. Can you taste the sugar?

ask.q: The sugar water looks just like plain water. Why does it taste sweet?
good: The sugar is still in there.
Tiny sugar particles are spread through all the water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: dissolved sugar is still there. What I saw: the sugar vanished, but the balance stayed level, and the water tasted sweet. Why: the sugar broke into particles too small to see, and they spread through the water. Every particle was still in the bottle.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make a balance from a coat hanger. You weigh sugar before and after it dissolves in a closed bottle, to find out if it is still there.

experiments.title: Lump, Grains or Powder: which sugar dissolves first?
experiments.question: Does the size of the pieces change how fast sugar dissolves?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which will dissolve first in water: a lump of kalkandu, ordinary sugar grains, or powdered sugar? Which will be last? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same glass, the same amount of water from the same jug, and about the same amount of sugar each time (one level teaspoon). Stir the same way: 5 slow stirs every 30 seconds. Only the size of the pieces changes. Water from one jug is all the same warmth.
results_table: Time until no pieces are left

materials.item: kalkandu (rock sugar, called mishri in Hindi), a few pieces about the size of a pea
ordinary sugar
powdered sugar, or sugar crushed with a rolling pin inside a folded sheet of paper
3 clear glasses or tumblers of the same size
a jug of water at room temperature, and a small cup to measure it
a teaspoon, and a phone or clock to time with

schedule.what: Dissolve a lump of kalkandu, sugar grains and powdered sugar, one at a time, and time each one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each kind of sugar, as tall as the number of minutes it took.

flow.do: 1. Make powdered sugar: fold 2 teaspoons of sugar inside a sheet of paper and press hard with a rolling pin. 2. Look at the three kinds of sugar side by side. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: These are all sugar, in different sizes. Which one will dissolve first? Which last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Crush some sugar with a rolling pin. Look at the lump, the grains and the powder. Which will dissolve first? Why?

ask.q: Which will dissolve first, and why?
good: The powder, because its pieces are smallest.
The lump, because it is one piece.

flow.context: This is the first step of the sugar race. You compare a lump of kalkandu, ordinary sugar and powdered sugar.

flow.do: 1. Pour one small cup of water into each glass. 2. Measure 1 level teaspoon of each sugar. For the kalkandu, choose pieces that fill a teaspoon about as full as the sugar.
flow.say: We use the same water, the same glasses and about the same amount of sugar. Only the size of the pieces is different.
flow.kid: Pour one cup of water into each glass. Measure one teaspoon of each sugar.
flow.parent: The kalkandu will not fill the spoon exactly. That is fine. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh about 4 grams of each instead.

flow.do: 1. Tip the powdered sugar into glass 1 and start the timer. 2. Stir 5 times slowly every 30 seconds. 3. Stop the timer when no powder is left at the bottom. 4. Write the time.
flow.say: Go! Stir slowly five times every 30 seconds. Shout stop when you can't see any powder.
flow.kid: Tip in the powder. Start the timer. Stir 5 times every 30 seconds. Shout stop when it is gone!
flow.parent: Powdered sugar usually goes in well under a minute.

flow.do: Do the same with the sugar grains in glass 2.
flow.say: Now do the same with the ordinary grains. Stir slowly five times every 30 seconds.
flow.kid: Now do the grains. Stir the same way. Shout stop when they are gone.
flow.parent: Grains usually take 1 to 3 minutes. Look from the side, against a dark cloth, to see the last few.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with the kalkandu in glass 3. 2. If pieces are still there after 15 minutes, stop and write 'more than 15 minutes'.
flow.say: Now the lump. This one may take a while. While we wait, watch the lump closely. Is it getting smaller from the outside, or from the middle?
flow.kid: Now do the kalkandu. Stir the same way. Watch the lump. Does it shrink from the outside or the middle?

ask.q: Is the lump shrinking from the outside or from the middle?
good: From the outside.
Its corners are getting round.

flow.parent: A pea-sized lump often takes 5 to 15 minutes. Its sharp corners go round first, because water reaches the corners from more sides.

flow.do: Look at the times together.
flow.say: Which was fastest? The same amount of sugar went in each glass. So why did the powder win?
flow.kid: Which was fastest? All three had the same sugar. Why did the powder win?

check.q: Why did the powdered sugar dissolve first?
options: Powdered sugar is a different kind of sugar
Its tiny pieces have much more outside, so water can pull off many particles at once
Powder is lighter, so it floats away
check.why: Water can only pull particles off the outside of a piece. Crushing the same sugar into powder gives it far more outside, so many more particles leave at once. Picking 'a different kind' is a fair guess, but you made the powder from the same sugar yourself. Picking 'floats away' is a fair guess too, because powder seems light, but the powder sank and dissolved.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they think, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: smaller pieces dissolve faster. What I saw: the powder went in 30 seconds, the grains in 2 minutes, the kalkandu in 12 minutes. Why: small pieces have more outside, and water pulls particles off the outside.

experiments.context: In this experiment you race three kinds of sugar: a lump of kalkandu, ordinary grains and powder. You find out why size matters.

activities.title: Where Did the Sugar Go? look, wonder and draw

materials.item: a clear glass of water
a teaspoon of sugar and a spoon to stir
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Watch sugar disappear in water. Guess where it went, and draw what might be in the water.

activities.record: Draw what you think the sugar water would look like if you could zoom in very, very close.

flow.do: 1. Put the glass on the table. 2. Let your child drop in the teaspoon of sugar and stir slowly. 3. Both of you watch until the grains are gone.
flow.say: Drop the sugar in and stir slowly. Watch it closely. Tell me what you notice.
flow.kid: Drop the sugar into the water. Stir slowly. Watch closely. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: The grains get smaller.
The water looks wobbly.
Where did it go?

flow.context: This is a quick start to the unit. You watch sugar disappear in water and wonder where it went.

flow.do: Ask where the sugar went, and listen to the whole answer.
flow.say: Where do you think the sugar went? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where do you think the sugar went? Is it still in the glass?
flow.parent: Common answers are 'it melted', 'it's gone' and 'it's hiding at the bottom'. Don't correct any of them yet. The experiments in this unit will test them. You will see a wobbly shimmer in the water while the sugar dissolves. That is sweet water bending light differently from plain water.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw what is in the water, as if they could zoom in very, very close.
flow.say: If you could shrink and swim in this water, what would you see? Draw it.
flow.kid: If you were tiny and swimming in this glass, what would you see? Draw it.
flow.think: If you can't see the sugar, how could you find out if it is still there?
flow.parent: Keep this drawing. At the end of the unit, your child can draw it again and compare.

activities.context: This is a quick look-and-wonder activity to start the unit. You watch sugar disappear and draw where you think it went.

activities.title: Zoom In on a Grain: sugar, salt and kalkandu

materials.item: a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in as far as it goes
a few grains of sugar, a few grains of salt and one piece of kalkandu
a sheet of black or dark paper
a rolling pin or a steel tumbler, and a folded sheet of paper

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass. It can hurt your eyes.

schedule.what: Look at sugar, salt and kalkandu up close. Crush some sugar and taste a pinch of the powder.

activities.record: Draw one sugar grain, one salt grain and the kalkandu, as big as you can, with their flat sides and corners.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a few sugar grains and salt grains on the dark paper, apart from each other. 2. Look at them with the magnifying glass, or take a zoomed-in photo with a phone.
flow.say: Look closely at one sugar grain. What shape is it? Does it have flat sides? Now look at the salt.
flow.kid: Look at one sugar grain up close. What shape is it? Now look at a salt grain. Are they the same?

ask.q: What do you see on the grains?
good: Flat sides and sharp corners.
The salt grains look like tiny boxes.

flow.parent: Each sugar grain is a small crystal, with flat shiny faces. Table salt grains are often tiny cubes, like dice. A phone photo, zoomed in on the screen afterwards, often shows this best.
flow.context: This is the first step of Zoom In on a Grain. You look closely at sugar and salt grains.

flow.do: Look at the kalkandu piece with and without the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Kalkandu is sugar too. It is a much bigger crystal. Can you see its flat faces?
flow.kid: Kalkandu is sugar too, in a big crystal. Find its flat faces.
flow.parent: A crystal has flat sides because its particles are stacked in neat rows, like bricks in a wall.

flow.do: 1. Fold a teaspoon of sugar inside paper. 2. Press and roll hard with the rolling pin. 3. Open it and look at the powder through the magnifying glass. 4. Taste a pinch.
flow.say: Now we crush it. Is the powder still sugar? How can we tell?
flow.kid: Crush sugar inside the paper with the rolling pin. Look at the powder. Taste a pinch. Is it still sugar?

check.q: You crushed sugar into powder so fine that the grains are hard to see. Is it still sugar?
options: Yes, it is still sweet, just in smaller pieces
No, crushing turns it into something else
Only the big pieces are sugar
check.why: Each tiny piece of powder is still made of sugar particles, so it still tastes sweet. If you could keep going, the smallest piece of sugar would be one sugar particle. Picking 'turns it into something else' is a fair thought, because the powder looks different, softer and whiter. But it tastes the same.

activities.context: In this activity you look at sugar, salt and kalkandu up close with a magnifying glass. Then you crush sugar into powder and check that it is still sugar.

activities.title: Sweet at the Bottom: does sugar spread by itself?

materials.item: a tall clear glass of water
3 teaspoons of sugar
2 clean drinking straws and 2 clean steel spoons

schedule.what: Put sugar at the bottom of a tall glass without stirring. Wait 30 minutes. Taste the top and the bottom. Then stir and taste again.

activities.record: Draw the glass. Write 'sweet' or 'plain' next to the top and the bottom, before and after stirring.

flow.do: 1. Fill the tall glass with water and let it stand still for a minute. 2. Gently tip 3 teaspoons of sugar into the water so it sinks to the bottom. 3. Do not stir. Put the glass where nobody will bump it. 4. Wait 30 minutes.
flow.say: We will leave the sugar at the bottom with no stirring. Will the top of the water get sweet by itself? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tip the sugar in gently. Don't stir! Will the top get sweet by itself? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Sweet at the Bottom. You leave sugar at the bottom of a tall glass to see if it spreads by itself.

flow.do: 1. Dip a clean straw just under the surface. 2. Press a finger tight on the top of the straw and lift it out. 3. Let the drops fall onto a clean spoon. 4. Taste.
flow.say: This is water from the very top. Taste it. Sweet or plain?
flow.kid: Dip a straw just under the top of the water. Press a finger on the top of the straw and lift it out. Let the drops fall onto a spoon. Taste them. Sweet or plain?
flow.parent: The straw trick: a finger pressed on the top end holds the water in the straw. Lift your finger and the water drops out. The top may taste very faintly sweet if pouring the sugar stirred the water a little. The bottom will still be much sweeter.

flow.do: 1. Press a finger on the top of the second straw. 2. Push it straight down to the very bottom. 3. Lift your finger for one second, then press it down again. 4. Lift the straw out and let the drops fall onto the second spoon. 5. Taste.
flow.say: Now take water from the very bottom. Keep your finger on the top of the straw until the straw is right at the bottom.
flow.kid: Press a finger on the top of the straw. Push it to the bottom. Lift your finger, then press again. Lift the straw out and taste the drops.

check.q: After 30 minutes, the top tasted plain and the bottom tasted very sweet. What does this show?
options: Sugar particles stay where they are and never move
Sugar particles do spread by themselves, but very slowly
The top water has no particles in it
check.why: Sugar particles are always moving, so they do spread out on their own. This spreading is called diffusion. But through water it is very slow: it would take many days to reach the top of the glass. Picking 'never move' is a fair reading of what you tasted, but in a few days the top would get sweet. Picking 'the top has no particles' forgets that the water itself is made of particles.

flow.do: Stir the glass 10 times. Then taste from the top again with a clean straw.
flow.say: Now stir it 10 times and taste the top again.
flow.kid: Stir 10 times. Taste the top again. What changed?

ask.q: Why is the top sweet now?
good: Stirring carried the sugar particles all through the water.

flow.parent: You may see a shimmering, clear layer at the bottom before stirring. That is the sweet water. It is heavier than plain water, so it stays at the bottom.

activities.context: In this activity you leave sugar at the bottom of a tall glass, without stirring, and taste the top and the bottom. It shows how slowly sugar particles spread on their own.

activities.title: Ask the Ants: can they find sugar we can't see?

materials.item: a small piece of card or a steel plate
a little sugar water (a teaspoon of sugar stirred into half a cup of water) and a little plain water
a teaspoon

activities.safety: Watch the ants, but don't touch them. Some ants bite.

schedule.what: Put a drop of sugar water and a drop of plain water near an ant trail. Check after 15 minutes and after 30 minutes.

activities.record: Draw the card with its two drops, and the ants you see at each one after 15 minutes and 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Find a place where ants walk, such as a window sill, the kitchen platform edge or the balcony. 2. Put a drop of sugar water at one end of the card and a drop of plain water at the other. 3. Mark which is which with a pencil. 4. Lay the card near the ants' path.
flow.say: Both drops look the same. Will the ants be able to tell them apart? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put a drop of sugar water at one end of the card and a drop of plain water at the other. They look the same. Can the ants tell them apart?
flow.wait: Check after 15 minutes, and again after 30 minutes
flow.parent: Ants need sugar for energy. A colony has many mouths to feed, so ants search all the time and lead each other to good food. If no ants come in 30 minutes, that is not a result: try near the bottom of a balcony wall or a potted plant, or try again another day.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask the Ants. You give ants a drop of sugar water and a drop of plain water that look the same.

flow.do: Check the card after 15 minutes, and again after 30 minutes. Count the ants at each drop. If no ants have come, move to another spot and wait again.
flow.say: Which drop did the ants go to? How did they know, when we can't see the sugar?
flow.kid: Count the ants at each drop. Which one did they choose?

check.q: Suppose the ants gather at the sugar water drop and leave the plain water alone. How did they find it?
options: They sensed the sugar particles with their antennae
check.why: Ants smell and taste with their antennae. When an ant touches the sugar water, her antennae pick up the sugar particles, so she can tell sugar water from plain water. Then she lays a scent trail so other ants can find it too. Picking 'they saw it' is a natural guess, but the sugar particles are too small for anyone to see. Picking 'luck' is worth testing: try again with the drops swapped.

flow.do: Wipe the card and the place where it lay clean with a wet cloth.
flow.say: The ants found sugar that our eyes could not see. Let's clean up so they don't follow it indoors.
flow.kid: The ants found the hidden sugar! Now wipe the drops away.
flow.think: What else might ants notice that we can't?

activities.context: In this activity you ask ants to find sugar you can't see. You put a drop of sugar water and a drop of plain water near their path.

projects.title: The Shrinking Camphor: a 7-day watch

materials.item: 2 camphor tablets of the same size (karpooram in Tamil, kapur in Hindi)
a small saucer, and a small glass jar with a lid
a sheet of paper and a pencil, to trace around the tablets

projects.safety: Camphor is poisonous if swallowed. A grown-up handles the tablets and keeps them out of reach of small children. Never light the camphor for this project. Wash your hands after touching it.

schedule.what: Trace both tablets. Put one on an open saucer and one in a closed jar, side by side, high up out of reach.
Trace the open tablet again on the same paper. Sniff the air near the saucer.
Trace the open tablet again. Look at the tablet in the jar without opening the jar.
Trace both tablets. Open the jar and sniff. Compare the two, and explain what happened.

projects.record: One sheet with the outlines of the open tablet on days 1, 3, 5 and 7, one inside the other, and the jar tablet on days 1 and 7.

flow.do: 1. Put both tablets on the paper and trace round each one. Write 'Day 1'. 2. Put one tablet on the saucer. 3. Put the other in the jar and close the lid. 4. Put both on a high shelf, side by side.
flow.say: Camphor is a solid. We will watch two tablets for a week: one in the open air, and one shut in a jar. Will either of them change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Trace both tablets. One goes on the saucer. One goes in the jar. A grown-up puts them up high. Will they change?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Shrinking Camphor, a 7-day project. You watch one camphor tablet in the open air and one in a closed jar.

flow.do: On day 3 and day 5, trace the open tablet on the same paper, inside the first outline. On day 5, also look at the jar tablet without opening the jar.
flow.say: Has the open tablet changed? Can you smell camphor near it?
flow.kid: Trace the open tablet again. Is it smaller? Can you smell it?
flow.wait: Do this on day 3 and day 5, about 5 minutes each time
flow.parent: In a warm, airy room the open tablet gets noticeably smaller within a few days, and its edges go soft and round. If it is changing slowly, keep going for a few more days.

flow.do: On day 7, trace both tablets. Then open the jar and sniff, holding it a little away from your nose.
flow.say: Compare the two tablets. Then smell inside the jar. Where did the missing camphor from the open tablet go? How do you know?
flow.kid: Trace both tablets. Open the jar and sniff, not too close. Where did the open tablet's camphor go?

ask.q: Where did the missing camphor from the open tablet go? How do you know?
good: Into the air, as camphor particles.
We could smell it in the room, and the saucer stayed dry.

flow.do: Talk about why the jar tablet hardly changed.
flow.say: The jar tablet hardly shrank, but the jar smelled strongly. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Why did the jar tablet stay big? Why did the jar smell so strong?

ask.q: Why did the tablet in the jar hardly shrink?
good: The particles could not get out of the jar.
The air in the jar got full of camphor particles.

flow.parent: In the jar, camphor particles leave the tablet too. But they cannot escape, so the air in the jar fills up with them. Soon as many go back onto the tablet as leave it, so it stops shrinking. That is why the jar smells so strong.

challenges.title: Prove It's There, Without Tasting
challenges.problem: A friend says the glass of sugar water on the table is just water, because he can't see any sugar. He won't taste it, because he says that's cheating. Find a way to show the sugar is there, without anyone tasting it.
constraints: You may use only things from home.
Your test must work with a glass that looks exactly like plain water.
materials: a glass of sugar water and a glass of plain water that look the same
a steel plate or a sheet of black paper
a kitchen scale, if you have one
general: Weigh it, if you have a kitchen scale. Take two glasses of the same kind. Fill each to the same mark, one with sugar water and one with plain water. Put them on the scale one at a time. The sugar water weighs a few grams more. Fill carefully, or the difference is lost.
Let it dry. Put a few drops of each on a steel plate in a sunny window. The plain water dries to almost nothing. The sugar water dries to a sticky patch.
Rub a drop of each between your finger and thumb, then let it dry. Sugar water makes your fingers sticky.
creative: With a brush, paint a few lines of each water on black paper. When the lines dry, the sugar lines may shine and feel stiff.
Dip a strip of kitchen paper in each water and let both dry. The sugar strip feels stiffer.
Ask a grown-up to boil a few spoons of each in a small pan until almost dry. The sugar water leaves a sticky, brownish syrup at the bottom.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own test. Draw it, try it, and show your friend the result.

flow.do: 1. Set out a glass of sugar water and a glass of plain water. 2. Read the problem aloud.
flow.say: A friend says this is just water, and he won't let anyone taste it. How could we show him the sugar is there?
flow.kid: A friend won't believe there is sugar in this glass. Nobody can taste it. How can you show him?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Prove It's There challenge. You find a way to show sugar is in water without tasting it.

flow.do: 1. Try two of the usual ideas. 2. Then try one of the creative ideas, or your own.
flow.say: Pick two ways to try. Which shows the sugar most clearly?
flow.kid: Pick two tests and try them. Which one shows the sugar best?
flow.parent: The boiling test needs a grown-up at the stove. Start the drying test first, on a steel plate in a sunny window. It may take an hour or more, so look at it again at the end, or later in the day.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain their best test, as if to the friend.
flow.say: Explain to your friend why your test shows the sugar is there.
flow.kid: Tell your friend what your test showed. Why does it prove the sugar is there?
flow.think: Which test would convince someone who doesn't believe you?

challenges.title: Quick Panakam: dissolve the jaggery fast
challenges.problem: Guests are arriving in 10 minutes, and you want to serve a jug of panakam, a cool South Indian drink made from jaggery, water, dry ginger and cardamom. The jaggery is one hard block. How will you get it dissolved in cold water in time?
constraints: The drink must be cool, so you can't boil the whole jug.
Use only things from your kitchen.
materials: a small block of jaggery, about the size of a matchbox
a grater, a rolling pin, a cloth and a steel tumbler
a spoon and a strainer or clean cloth
a pinch of dry ginger powder (sukku) and cardamom powder, if you have them
general: Grate or crush the jaggery first, so it has much more outside for the water to reach.
Stir all the time, so fresh water keeps reaching the jaggery.
Dissolve the jaggery in a small cup of warm water first, then pour it into the cold water.
creative: Put crushed jaggery and water in a closed bottle and shake it hard.
Wrap the jaggery in a clean cloth and pound it with a rolling pin, then drop the cloth bundle in the water and squeeze it.
Ask a grown-up to chop the block into small cubes with a knife before you start.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own fastest way. Time it. Then strain the panakam, add a pinch of dry ginger and cardamom, and serve it.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the jaggery block. 2. Read the problem aloud. 3. Ask them to plan before touching anything.
flow.say: Think about the Lump, Grains or Powder race, where you timed three kinds of sugar. What made the sugar dissolve fastest? How can we use that for the jaggery?
flow.kid: Look at the jaggery block. Remember the Lump, Grains or Powder race. What made the sugar dissolve fastest? Make a plan.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Quick Panakam challenge. You plan the fastest way to dissolve jaggery for a drink.

flow.do: 1. Crush or grate the jaggery. 2. Start the timer. 3. Add it to the water and stir, following your plan.
flow.say: Start the timer. Let's see if your plan beats 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Crush the jaggery. Start the timer. Stir it in. Can you beat 10 minutes?
flow.parent: A grown-up handles the grater, because it can cut fingers. Jaggery has some tiny bits of sugarcane and dust that never dissolve. So strain the panakam through a clean cloth or a fine strainer before serving.

flow.do: 1. Strain the drink. 2. Add a pinch of dry ginger and cardamom. 3. Taste and talk about what worked.
flow.say: Which part of your plan helped most? Why?
flow.kid: Strain it. Add the spices. Taste! Which part of your plan helped most?

ask.q: Why did crushing the jaggery help so much?
good: Small pieces have more outside, so water reaches more particles at once.
