quiz.p: What is everything around you made of?
opts: Particles only in solids, not in water or air
Particles far too small to see, in solids, liquids and gases
Grains you can see with a magnifying glass
quiz.why: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of particles far too small to see. Picking 'only in solids' means thinking water and air are smooth all the way down, with no pieces. Picking 'grains you can see' confuses grains, which are huge heaps of particles, with particles.

quiz.p: You stir sugar into water and the grains disappear. Where is the sugar now?
opts: Spread through the water as tiny sugar particles
quiz.why: The sugar broke into particles too small to see, and they spread among the water particles. Picking 'destroyed' is the most common guess, because we trust our eyes. Picking 'turned into water' misses that the water tastes sweet: the sugar is still sugar.

quiz.p: On a kitchen scale, a closed bottle of water and a packet of sugar weigh 120 grams together. You pour the sugar into the bottle, close it and shake it until the sugar is gone. You put the bottle and the empty packet back on the scale. What does the scale show?
quiz.why: Every sugar particle is still in the bottle, so the weight stays the same. Picking 'less' means thinking dissolved sugar weighs nothing. Picking 'more' is a guess that sugar water is heavier than water and sugar apart, but nothing was added.

quiz.p: In the hanger balance test, why did we first lift the sugar packet out of the bag and watch the straw?
opts: To check that the balance could feel the weight of the sugar
To let the sugar cool down
To make the test go faster
quiz.why: If the balance moved when the packet was lifted out, we knew it could feel the sugar. So when it did not move after dissolving, we knew the sugar had not lost any weight.

quiz.p: Which dissolves fastest in a glass of water?
quiz.why: Powder has the most outside, so water can pull off many particles at once. Picking kalkandu means thinking a bigger piece holds more and so goes faster, but it has the least outside.

quiz.p: You want to test whether stirring makes sugar dissolve faster. What should you keep the same?
opts: The water, the glass and the amount of sugar
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes, here the stirring. Everything else stays the same, so you know the stirring made the difference.

quiz.p: Which of these is melting, not dissolving?
opts: Ghee turning runny in a warm pan
quiz.why: Ghee turns liquid because it is heated, with nothing else added. That is melting. Salt in rasam and sugar in cold milk are dissolving: they break up in a liquid, with no heat needed.

quiz.p: Someone says, 'Sugar melts in tea because the tea is hot.' What is wrong with this?
opts: Sugar dissolves even in cold water, so it is dissolving, not melting
quiz.why: Sugar dissolves in ice-cold water too. Melting sugar needs a dry pan at about 186 degrees Celsius. Hot tea only makes dissolving faster.

quiz.p: Some people once said that when silver dissolves in a strong acid, the silver stops existing. Which result would show they were wrong?
opts: Getting the same silver back out of the acid
quiz.why: If the silver had stopped existing, nobody could get it back. So it must have been there all along, as tiny particles. A doctor called Daniel Sennert did this in the 1600s.

quiz.p: Sugar was left at the bottom of a tall glass with no stirring. After 30 minutes, how did the top taste?
opts: Plain, because sugar particles spread very slowly by themselves
quiz.why: Sugar particles do move by themselves, but through water this spreading is very slow. It could take days to reach the top. Picking 'sugar rises' is a fair guess, but sweet water is heavier, so it stays at the bottom.

quiz.p: Ants went to a drop of sugar water and left a drop of plain water alone. The drops looked the same. How did the ants know?
opts: They sensed the sugar particles with their antennae
quiz.why: Ants smell and taste with their antennae. When an ant touches the sugar water, she picks up the sugar particles and knows it is food. Nobody can see dissolved sugar.

items.p: You drop a spoon of salt into a glass of water and stir. The salt disappears. Which word says what happened?
items.why: Salt breaking up in water and spreading through it is dissolving. Melting needs heat. Evaporating is a liquid going into the air.

items.p: Which of these is made of particles?
items.why: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of particles. Picking only the stone means thinking only hard things have pieces.

items.p: Why can't we see sugar particles?
items.why: A sugar particle is about a millionth of a millimetre across, far too small for eyes or ordinary microscopes.

items.p: In the hanger balance test, what happened to the straw pointer when the sugar dissolved?
items.why: The sugar was still in the bottle, so the weight did not change and the balance stayed level.

items.p: A sugar grain has flat sides and sharp corners. What is a solid like this called?
items.why: A crystal has its particles stacked in neat rows, which gives it flat sides. A solution is the mixture you get after dissolving.

items.p: When sugar dissolves in water, it is gone for ever.
items.why: False. The sugar is still there as particles. You can taste it and weigh it.

items.p: Sugar can dissolve in cold water.
items.why: True. It dissolves more slowly in cold water, but it does dissolve. No heat is needed.

items.p: Powdered sugar is a different substance from ordinary sugar.
items.why: False. It is the same sugar, crushed into smaller pieces. It tastes the same.

items.p: The clear mixture you get when sugar dissolves in water is called a ____.
items.why: Sugar water and salty water are solutions.

items.p: Sugar dissolves faster when it is crushed, when it is ____, and when the water is warm.
items.why: Stirring carries the sweet water away from the sugar, so fresh water can reach it.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a very tiny piece that things are made of
break up and spread through a liquid
a solid with particles in neat rows
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Sort these. Is it dissolving or melting?
items.why: Dissolving needs a liquid to break the solid up. Melting needs heat, and nothing else.

items.p: A friend says the sugar in her tea has disappeared. How could she find out if it is still there? Give one way.
items.a: She could taste the tea to see if it is sweet. Or she could weigh the cup and the sugar before and after.
items.why: A strong answer names a real test, such as tasting, weighing or asking ants, and says what result would show the sugar is there.

items.p: Why does a glass of sugar water taste sweet everywhere after you stir it?
items.a: Stirring spreads the sugar particles through all the water, so every sip has some.
items.why: A strong answer mentions particles spreading through the whole glass.

items.p: Draw what you think sugar water would look like if you could zoom in very close. Show the water particles and the sugar particles.
items.a: Many small circles for water particles, with a few different circles for sugar particles spread out among them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sugar spread out among the water, not sitting in one lump.
items.art: A large empty circle, like the view through a magnifying glass.

items.p: Why does a lump of kalkandu dissolve more slowly than the same amount of powdered sugar?
opts: The lump has much less outside for the water to reach
items.why: Water pulls particles off the outside only. A lump has little outside compared with powder. Picking 'not real sugar' misses that kalkandu is crystals of ordinary sugar.

items.p: In the Lump, Grains or Powder race, why did we use water from one jug for all three glasses?
opts: So all the water was the same warmth
items.why: Warm water dissolves sugar faster. Water from one jug is all the same warmth, so only the size of the sugar pieces changed.

items.p: Which of these shows that particles move by themselves?
opts: Sugar sits at the bottom and never changes
Sugar slowly makes the water above it sweet, even with no stirring
A stone stays where you put it
items.why: Over days, sugar particles keep moving and spread up through the water by themselves. A stone's particles move too, but they jiggle in place.

items.p: When a sugar grain dissolves, which particles leave first?
items.why: Water can only reach the outside of the grain, so the outside particles leave first. That is why corners go round first.

items.p: The tablet of camphor in a closed jar hardly shrank in a week. Why?
opts: The camphor particles could not escape, so the air in the jar filled up with them
items.why: Particles leave the tablet in the jar too. But they stay trapped, so soon as many go back onto the tablet as leave it.

items.p: A sugar particle is the smallest piece of sugar there can be.
items.why: True. Break a sugar particle and you get atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which are not sugar.

items.p: Dissolved sugar weighs less, because it is spread out.
items.why: False. Every particle still weighs what it did. The hanger balance stayed level.

items.p: The slow spreading of particles by themselves, with no stirring, is called ____.
items.why: Diffusion is why the sugar at the bottom of the tall glass would, after many days, reach the top.

items.p: Put the hanger balance test in order.
items: Dissolve the sugar in bottle A and shake
Balance bottle A and the sugar packet against bottle B
Put the bottle and the empty paper back, and look at the pointer
Make the hanger balance with a straw pointer
a: Make the hanger balance with a straw pointer
Balance bottle A and the sugar packet against bottle B
Dissolve the sugar in bottle A and shake
Put the bottle and the empty paper back, and look at the pointer
items.why: First make the balance, then balance the sides, then dissolve, then weigh again with everything back in the bag.

items.p: Sort these. Does it make sugar dissolve faster, or make no difference?
items: using a blue glass instead of a clear one
items.why: Smaller pieces, stirring and warmth change how fast particles leave the sugar. The colour of the glass or words said over it change nothing.

items.p: Explain to a younger child why crushing jaggery helps it dissolve faster. Use the word 'outside'.
items.a: Water can only pull bits off the outside of a piece. When you crush the jaggery, there are many small pieces with lots more outside, so it dissolves faster.
items.why: A strong answer says water works on the outside, and crushing makes more outside.

items.p: In Sweet at the Bottom, sugar was left at the bottom of a tall glass without stirring. After 30 minutes the top tasted plain and the bottom tasted sweet. What would you expect if you left the glass for a whole week without stirring? Why?
items.a: The top would slowly get sweeter, because sugar particles keep moving and spread out bit by bit.
items.why: A strong answer says the particles keep moving and slowly spread, even with no stirring.

items.p: Ants found the sugar water drop, though it looked exactly like the plain water drop. Why is this good evidence that the sugar was still there?
items.a: The ants sense sugar with their antennae, and they only went to one drop. So that drop really had sugar in it, even though we couldn't see it.
items.why: A strong answer says the ants could tell the drops apart, so something real was different.

items.p: Draw a sugar grain as a block of particles. Then draw it again after one minute in water, with some particles pulled off.
items.a: The second drawing shows a smaller block, with rounded corners, and loose particles spread among water particles.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the outside particles leaving first.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled 'Before' and 'After one minute'.

items.p: Divya and her grandmother Kamala disagree about the sugar in Kamala's coffee.

views.says: I always stir my coffee a lot. If you don't stir, the sugar stays at the bottom and the first sips aren't sweet.
Stirring isn't needed. Particles move by themselves, so the sugar will spread through the coffee anyway.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from one of your tests. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Kamala for drinking now, using the tall glass test, where the top stayed plain after 30 minutes. It also says Divya is right that particles move by themselves, but the spreading is far too slow for a cup of coffee.
items.why: Both have a point. Particles do spread by themselves, as Divya says. But it takes days, so Kamala's stirring is what makes the first sip sweet.

items.p: You put a camphor tablet in an empty jar, close the lid tight, and weigh the jar every day for a week. What happens to the weight of the closed jar?
items.why: Some camphor particles leave the tablet, but they stay in the air inside the closed jar. Nothing escapes, so the total weight stays the same.

items.p: You put 4 teaspoons of sugar into a full glass of water. Will the water spill over the top?
opts: No, the sugar takes up no space at all
A little may spill, because the sugar particles still take up some space
It will spill a whole cupful
items.why: Sugar particles are still there, so they take up some room. The level rises a little. A heap of sugar on a spoon also has air between the grains, so the rise is less than the size of the heap.

items.p: Which test would best show that dissolved salt is still in water, without tasting?
opts: Letting a few drops dry on a clean steel plate
items.why: When the water goes into the air, the salt particles stay behind and gather into white grains again. Looking cannot work, because the particles are too small to see.

items.p: In the old days, some scientists said particles were not real because nobody could see one. What is the problem with that reason?
opts: Nothing, it is a good reason
Many real things are too small to see, and we can find them in other ways
Particles are big enough to see
items.why: Tasting, weighing and the ants all found sugar we could not see. Not being able to see something does not show it is not there.

items.p: If you could keep cutting a grain of sugar in half, you would always get smaller sugar.
items.why: False. After about 60 cuts, each halving the amount, you would reach one sugar particle. Cut that, and you get atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which are not sugar.

items.p: The rule that the total weight stays the same in a closed bottle, whatever changes happen inside, is called the conservation of ____.
items.why: Mass means how much stuff there is. It is never lost, only moved or changed.

items.p: Put these in order, from the slowest to dissolve to the fastest.
items: Powdered sugar in warm water, stirred
A kalkandu lump in cold water, not stirred
Sugar grains in cold water, stirred
a: A kalkandu lump in cold water, not stirred
Sugar grains in cold water, stirred
Powdered sugar in warm water, stirred
items.why: Big pieces, cold water and no stirring are slowest. Small pieces, warm water and stirring are fastest.

items.p: Someone did the hanger balance test, but did not put the empty sugar paper back in the bag. Side A went up a tiny bit. They said, 'Dissolved sugar weighs less!' What went wrong?
items.a: The paper was left out, so side A lost the paper's weight. That is why it went up. To be fair, everything that was on side A before must go back.
items.why: A strong answer spots that the test was not fair: something was taken away.

items.p: Sugar dissolves in water, but sand does not. What do you think is different about how water particles treat sugar particles and sand particles?
items.a: Water particles attract sugar particles strongly enough to pull them off the grain. Sand particles hold on to each other more tightly than water can pull, so they stay together.
items.why: A strong answer says dissolving depends on a pull between the water and the solid. Any good guess counts, even if not every detail is known.

items.p: Your body gets energy from a sugar called glucose, carried in your blood. Why is it useful that this sugar is dissolved, and not in grains?
items.a: Dissolved sugar is spread out as tiny particles, so the blood can carry it everywhere and it can get into every cell. Grains would be too big and would block thin tubes.
items.why: A strong answer links dissolving to how easily tiny particles can travel and get into cells.

items.p: A grain of sugar holds roughly a million million million particles. Why does it still look like one solid grain, and not a cloud of dots?
items.a: The particles are packed tightly and hold on to each other in neat rows. They are far too small for our eyes to see one by one, so we only see the whole grain.
items.why: A strong answer mentions that the particles are packed close and are too small to see apart.

items.p: You want to find out if warm water makes sugar dissolve faster. Plan a fair test. Say what you change and what you keep the same.
items.a: Change only the warmth of the water: one glass of cool water and one of warm water. Keep the same glass, the same amount of water, the same amount and kind of sugar, and the same stirring. Time how long each takes.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, the warmth, and names several things kept the same.

items.p: In the camphor project, the tablet in the closed jar hardly shrank. Someone says this shows the camphor in the jar stopped moving. Is that right? Explain.
items.a: No. The camphor particles in the jar keep leaving the tablet, but just as many land back on it, because they can't escape. So the tablet stays the same size, even though its particles are moving all the time.
items.why: A strong answer separates 'nothing changes that we can see' from 'nothing is moving'.

items.p: Draw the hanger balance three times: with the sugar packet beside bottle A, with the packet lifted out, and after the sugar dissolved. Show the straw each time.
items.a: First drawing: the straw is at the line. Second drawing: side A is higher and the straw has swung away from the line. Third drawing: the straw is back at the line.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the balance could feel the sugar, and that dissolving did not change the weight.
items.art: Three empty frames side by side.

items.p: Three people talk about how we know particles are real.

views.says: Nobody has ever seen a particle. Science should only talk about what we can measure, such as weight and heat.

views.who: Daniel Sennert, a doctor, in the 1600s
views.says: Silver dissolved in acid came back as the same silver. So it must have been there all along, as particles too small to see.
Today we have special microscopes that make pictures of single atoms. But most of what we know about particles still comes from tests like weighing and tasting.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and why? Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view with a reason, for example Sennert's, because getting the silver back is strong evidence even without seeing. It also says what another view gets right, for example that Ostwald was right to ask for evidence, and he did change his mind when it came.
items.why: Each view has a point. Ostwald asked for evidence, Sennert found indirect evidence, and the chemist today shows that both seeing and testing count.

applications: ORS, the oral rehydration drink given for diarrhoea, is salt and sugar dissolved in clean water. It has saved millions of lives.
Sugar mills boil sugarcane juice until the water leaves and the sugar particles gather into crystals again.
Sharbats, filter coffee, payasam and the syrup that rasgullas sit in all depend on sugar dissolving.
Many medicines are dissolved in water or in syrup, so the body can take them in quickly.
Washing powder dissolves in water, so it can reach the dirt in every thread of the cloth.
Water purifiers that use RO remove the salts dissolved in tap or borewell water.
Kokum sharbat from the Konkan coast is made by dissolving sugar in kokum juice.

open_questions.q: Is there a smallest thing, with nothing smaller inside it?
open_questions.why_open: Sugar particles are made of atoms, and atoms of smaller particles. Physicists do not know if there is a last, smallest level.

open_questions.q: Exactly why do some things dissolve in water and others do not?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists understand the main reasons, but working out from scratch how much of a new substance will dissolve is still very hard. They often have to test it.

open_questions.q: What happens at the very moment a single particle leaves a crystal?
open_questions.why_open: It happens in far less than a millionth of a second. Scientists study it with computer models, and they are still learning the details.

open_questions.q: How do ants tell sugar from other things so quickly with their antennae?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know ants have many sensing cells on their antennae, but how an ant puts the signals together to choose food is still being studied.

maths.context: This is about the hanger balance test. You weighed a bottle of water with a packet of sugar beside it, then dissolved the sugar and weighed again.
maths.problem: On a kitchen scale, a bottle of water weighs 115 grams and a packet of sugar weighs 16 grams. You dissolve the sugar in the bottle, then put the bottle and the empty packet on the scale together. What will the scale show? Explain how you know before you weigh it.
maths.explain: Before: 115 + 16 = 131 grams. When the sugar dissolves, every sugar particle is still in the bottle, and the paper is still on the scale. Nothing is added or taken away, so the scale still shows 131 grams.
maths.why_maths: Adding the weights first lets you predict the answer, so the scale can test your prediction.

maths.context: This is about the sugar race. You timed a kalkandu lump, ordinary sugar grains and powdered sugar dissolving in water.
maths.problem: In a sugar race, the sugar grains took 2 minutes to dissolve and the kalkandu lump took 12 minutes. How many times as long did the lump take?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 2 is 6. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12. So the lump took 6 times as long as the grains, though both were one teaspoon of the same sugar.

chart.title: Minutes to dissolve in the sugar race (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'six times as long' tells us how big the difference is, which 'slower' alone does not.

maths.context: This is about the camphor project. You traced a camphor tablet on an open saucer every two days to see if it shrank.
maths.problem: An open camphor tablet was 20 millimetres wide on day 1, 17 millimetres on day 3, and 14 millimetres on day 5. If it keeps shrinking the same way, how wide will it be on day 7? On which day will it be about 5 millimetres wide?
maths.answer: 11 millimetres on day 7. About 5 millimetres on day 11.
maths.explain: It loses 3 millimetres every 2 days: 20, 17, 14. So day 7 is 14 - 3 = 11. Then day 9 is 8, and day 11 is 5. A real tablet may not shrink at exactly the same rate, so this is a prediction to test.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern in the numbers lets you predict what will happen next, and then check it.

maths.context: This is about the Quick Panakam challenge, where you dissolve jaggery to make a drink for guests.
maths.problem: Each glass of panakam needs 3 tablespoons of grated jaggery. A family wants 6 glasses. How many tablespoons of jaggery do you need? If you crush it into small pieces, does the amount change?
maths.answer: 18 tablespoons. Crushing does not change the amount of jaggery, only the size of the pieces.
maths.explain: 6 groups of 3 is 6 x 3 = 18 tablespoons. Crushing breaks the jaggery into more, smaller pieces, but the total amount of jaggery stays the same. It just dissolves faster.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells you how much to prepare before the guests arrive, so you don't run out.

roots.context: We have learned that sugar breaks into particles in water and is still all there. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the hanger balance test, you dissolved sugar in a closed bottle of water and it vanished. Yet the balance stayed level and the water tasted sweet. The sugar had come apart into separate particles, far too small to see. Each of those particles is still sugar. A heap of sugar is many sugar particles packed together, and water can spread them out.
deep_truth.habit: We think of sugar as the white grains in the dabba, so when the grains vanish we say the sugar is gone. But grains are only how sugar particles are packed. Spread out in water, it is all the same sugar.
deep_truth.evidence: In the hanger balance test, bottle A weighed the same after the sugar vanished. Every sip from the stirred bottle tasted sweet. Ants went to the clear sugar water drop and left the plain one. Crushed sugar powder still tasted sweet.

three.who_am_i: You are made of particles too: water, sugars, fats and many more, far too small to see.
three.what_is_life: Your blood carries a sugar called glucose dissolved in it, to give every cell energy. Ants drink sugar dissolved in nectar and sweet juices.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything around you, the air, the sea and the stone floor, is made of particles, and they never stop moving.

roots.thread: Before you stirred, the sugar was one heap you could hold in a spoon. In water it became countless particles spread through the whole bottle, and none was lost. Boil cane juice in a sugar mill, and the particles gather into grains again. The heap and the spread-out particles are the same sugar, arranged in two ways.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water overnight. In the morning he asks for the salt, but Shvetaketu cannot find it. 'Taste the water from the top, the middle and the bottom,' says Uddalaka. Each time it is salty. 'You cannot see the salt, but it is there,' he says. 'In the same way, the finest essence is in everything, and you are that.'
teachings.link: This is the tasting test from your unit, told more than 2,000 years ago. Your test also showed something the story leaves out: unstirred, dissolved sugar stays mostly at the bottom, so the water must be stirred to taste the same everywhere.

teachings.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, Book 1, about lines 265 to 328
teachings.teaching: Lucretius, a Roman poet, said nature works through bodies too small to see. Clothes hung by the sea get damp, and dry again in the sun, but nobody sees the water come or go. A ring worn on a finger grows thinner over the years.
teachings.link: The camphor tablet and the drying clothes are the same kind of evidence. We see what particles do, not the particles themselves.

other_view.view: The salt story in the Upanishad is a teaching about the self, not about chemistry. Dissolving shows only that sugar particles spread through water. It does not show that one hidden essence fills everything.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The hanger balance uses small bottles with only one cup of water each, so 4 teaspoons of sugar (about 16 grams) tip it clearly. The straw pointer makes small tilts easy to see. The step that lifts the sugar packet out proves the balance can feel the sugar before the real test. The bottle stays capped while the sugar dissolves, so nothing escapes, and the paper goes back in the bag. A kitchen scale is offered as an option, not needed. The sugar race does one glass at a time, so one child can stir and time alone, and it stops at 15 minutes if the kalkandu is slow. Kalkandu is cheap at any kirana. The tall glass test was checked against how slowly sugar spreads in still water: the top stays plain for hours. The ant test says where to look and to wait longer if no ants come. The camphor project keeps tablets high up and never lit, because camphor is poisonous if swallowed. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 80 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a dissolved thing is still there, when nobody could see it? This card tells how.
how_we_found_out.who: Daniel Sennert, a German doctor, and later Robert Boyle, an English scientist
how_we_found_out.when: The early 1600s (Sennert), and later in the 1600s (Boyle)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: When two things truly mix, each stops being itself, and a new thing takes the place of both. So dissolved silver would no longer be silver.
how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, many teachers in Europe followed the Greek thinker Aristotle. They taught that when two things truly mix, each stops being itself. A new thing takes the place of both. So silver dissolved in a liquid would no longer be silver. In the early 1600s, Daniel Sennert, a German doctor who taught at Wittenberg, tested this. He dissolved silver in aqua fortis, a strong acid that eats into metal. The silver disappeared. Then he added another substance to the liquid, and the silver came out again as a fine powder. When he heated the powder, he had ordinary silver once more. Sennert said the silver had never stopped being silver. It had only broken into particles too small to see, and they had come together again. Later in the 1600s, the English scientist Robert Boyle used tests like this to argue that everything is made of tiny particles. Today we know they were right.
